Theodoric
thee-OD-uh-rik
proper noun
Theodoric the Great, king of the Ostrogoths (c. 454–526), an Arian ruler of Italy after the fall of Rome.

📖 Biblical Definition

Theodoric the Great was king of the Ostrogoths and ruler of Italy from 493 to 526, in the generations after the fall of the western Roman Empire. A capable and, for much of his reign, tolerant ruler, he kept order, patronized learning, and let the Roman administration continue; but he was an Arian in religion, holding the heresy that denied the full and eternal deity of the Son, confessing Him a creature rather than very God of very God. Under Arian Gothic rule the orthodox Catholic population of Italy lived as subjects of a heretical king. Theodoric’s reign darkened toward its end with suspicion and persecution: he imprisoned and put to death the philosopher Boethius, who wrote his great Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution, and the senator Symmachus, and he troubled the orthodox church. Theodoric stands in history as an example of the Germanic Arian kingdoms that ruled the ruins of the Roman West, holding a sub-Christian christology until they were brought, over generations, to the orthodox confession of the Son’s full deity. The dictionary names Theodoric’s Arianism as the same corruption the church condemned at Nicaea—the denial of the Son’s true and eternal Godhead—and honors the orthodox confession that prevailed against it: that the Son is of one substance with the Father, very God of very God, begotten not made, by whom all things were made.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Arian king of the Ostrogoths (c. 454–526) who ruled Italy; an able but heretical ruler whose Arianism denied the Son’s full deity, the error condemned at Nicaea.

THEODORIC, Arian king of the Ostrogoths, ruler of Italy (493–526).

Able and largely tolerant, he kept order and patronized learning.

An Arian, denying the full and eternal deity of the Son.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Theodoric’s Arianism is sometimes softened as mere political religion; it was the Nicene-condemned heresy that denied the Son’s true and eternal Godhead.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the tendency to soften Theodoric’s Arianism into a matter of mere political or ethnic religion—the Goths’ tribal creed, of no great doctrinal weight—or to praise his tolerance so warmly that the gravity of the heresy he held is lost. But Arianism was no trifle; it was the very error the church condemned at Nicaea in 325, the denial that the Son is true and eternal God, confessing Him instead a creature, however exalted.

The principle to recover is the full deity of the Son against the Arian denial. Scripture is plain: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God (John 1:1); by Him were all things created (Col 1:16)—and the Creator is no creature; before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58), the Son taking to Himself the divine name; we look for the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ (Tit 2:13). Arianism, whether in Theodoric’s Gothic kingdom or in its modern revivals, strikes at the heart of the gospel, for a Christ who is not truly God cannot truly save. The dictionary honors the Nicene confession that prevailed: the Son is of one substance with the Father, very God of very God, begotten not made—the faith against which Theodoric’s Arianism, for all his earthly ability, stood condemned.
